clue.text: Random investigation carried out in skin clinic?

definitions.text: Random investigation carried out in skin clinic?

parts.words: Random investigation carried out in skin clinic?
parts.note: an unannounced inspection, pictured as a dermatologist examining a pimple

explanation.surface: A dermatology clinic undergoes an unannounced inspection.
explanation.walkthrough: A spot is a pimple, so a skin clinic would literally check spots; the phrase also means a random inspection.
explanation.definitionFit: An unannounced inspection of a sample is the everyday sense; the skin clinic adds a pimple examination.

clue.text: Tap on green

parts.note: a gentle golf stroke played on the ... surface, read as if a tap were a faucet

explanation.definitionFit: On a golf course a light stroke towards the hole on the smooth turf is this shot.

clue.text: Well pitched-up delivery from J. C. Harris .

definitions.text: Well pitched-up delivery from J. C. Harris

parts.words: Well pitched-up delivery from J. C. Harris
parts.note: a cricket ball 'well pitched up' read as an infant thoroughly smeared in pitch, the figure in Joel Chandler Harris's Uncle Remus stories

explanation.surface: A cricket commentator praises a full-length ball bowled by someone called Harris.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a pitched-up delivery is a full-length ball; here 'pitched' means coated in pitch and 'delivery' is a newborn. Joel Chandler Harris wrote the Uncle Remus tale of Br'er Rabbit and the sticky doll.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Uncle Remus stories the sticky doll of pitch that traps Br'er Rabbit is this figure.

clue.text: … bowler, perhaps, holds in a little on his home ground

indicators.note: the hat 'holds in' the small amount, so the second piece sits inside the first

parts.note: a bowler is a kind of hat, so 'perhaps' marks an example
a little means a bit, here written as one run

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue, a cricket bowler keeps something back at his home ground.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries over the cricket of the previous clue, so 'bowler' looks like a cricketer; it is the hat, and 'holds in' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal's natural home territory is its natural environment.

clue.text: 10l put up in a storm

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as '10l put up in a storm (4)': '10l' is an OCR garble of the opening word(s), no scan, and a quoted search found nothing; likely a storm cone signal but the printed clue is missing.

clue.text: Highly esteemed idea for oilfield?

definitions.meaning: a notion an oil prospector might have, a thought about a well

explanation.surface: Someone praises a respected proposal for developing an oilfield.
explanation.definitionFit: Being held in high regard is the plain sense; an oil well considered in the mind gives the second, whimsical reading.

clue.text: Sweeter Welsh lamb?

parts.note: hill-grazed lamb from the uplands of Wales, said to taste sweeter, a grown hill-grazing ewe

explanation.surface: A butcher boasts that Welsh lamb tastes sweeter.
explanation.walkthrough: Welsh lamb is famed for grazing on hills, which is said to sweeten its meat; the question mark warns the answer describes the animal rather than the meat.
explanation.definitionFit: Lamb reared on Welsh hills comes from flocks grazing high upland pasture.

clue.text: Bird with young on open country-absurd contrivance

indicators.note: in an across clue 'on' means the bird and child come after the land

parts.note: a heath is open uncultivated land
a robin is a common garden bird
a son is someone's young offspring

explanation.surface: A bird and its chick sit out on the moor.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash separates wordplay from the definition. William Heath Robinson was a British cartoonist who drew ludicrously elaborate machines, so his name became a byword for them.
explanation.definitionFit: The cartoonist's name serves as an adjective for any ludicrously complicated, makeshift contraption.

clue.text: Having strong dialect, actors appear in " The Archers" for instance

parts.note: a broad accent is a strong regional one
the actors in a production are its cast

explanation.surface: The voice actors in a radio soap all speak in heavy regional accents.
explanation.walkthrough: The Archers is a long-running BBC radio soap set in a farming village, famous for its rural accents; 'appear in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A radio programme transmitted to listeners is an example of a transmission.

clue.text: Declare simple dive

parts.note: to declare something is to speak it
simple means easy

explanation.surface: Someone announces that a dive is an easy one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dive' looks like a diving move, but it means a seedy bar, like the illegal drinking dens of US Prohibition.
explanation.definitionFit: A dive is a disreputable bar, and an illicit Prohibition drinking den was exactly that.

clue.text: Nasty sound in unilateral emphysema

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, running across the word break

explanation.surface: A doctor hears a nasty noise in a patient with lung disease on one side.
explanation.definitionFit: A rattling crackle heard through a stethoscope in diseased lungs is a nasty breathing noise.

clue.text: Smack makes sense

definitions.meaning: a smack is a slight flavour, as in a smack of garlic
one of the five senses, that of the tongue

explanation.surface: A slap makes sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack can mean a faint flavour, and the faculty of the tongue is one of the five senses.

clue.text: Moves television camera backwards for photograph

indicators.note: the word for swinging a camera is read from end to start

parts.note: to pan is to swing a camera sideways, so 'moves' it this way gives pans

explanation.surface: A TV camera operator swings round to take a photograph.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick informal photograph is a snapshot, shortened.

clue.text: Warrant loses weight in this Scottish isle

indicators.note: the word warrant drops some of its letters

explanation.surface: A legal document gets lighter on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses' takes W and T, which are not side by side, from WARRANT. Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde, off Scotland's west coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The island in the Firth of Clyde is a Scottish isle, named here by 'this'.

clue.text: Point of view that is often obtuse

definitions.meaning: a slant or perspective on something
a geometric figure between two lines, which may be wider than ninety degrees

explanation.surface: Someone's opinion is often stupid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obtuse' looks like 'dim-witted', but it is the geometry term for more than ninety degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: A perspective on a story is a slant, and in geometry the figure between two lines can be obtuse.

clue.text: Article to receive trashy pieces?

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: the word trashy is broken in pieces and rearranged

explanation.surface: A receptacle made for junk.
explanation.walkthrough: As a whole the clue describes a receptacle for cigarette ends and ash, the trashy pieces; 'to receive' links A with the anagram SHTRAY of TRASHY.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish for stubs and ash collects smokers' rubbish.

clue.text: Beat sailor with a flourish

parts.note: to tan someone is to beat them
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: A sailor is thrashed with great ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flourish' is a fanfare of trumpets, not a wave of the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A fanfare of trumpets is a musical flourish.

clue.text: After a hundred, as old as we are, we need spirit

indicators.note: the age phrase comes after the hundred

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
our age is the age we are now

explanation.surface: A cricketer reaching a century in later life needs pluck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as old as we are' gives OUR AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirit here means pluck or bravery.

clue.text: Ban for English doctor on Greek ship

parts.note: MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor's degree
the Argo was Jason's ship in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A ban is imposed on an English doctor aboard a Greek vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: The Argo carried Jason and the Argonauts.
explanation.definitionFit: An official prohibition on trade is a ban.

clue.text: Otherwise license the rest of Hamlet

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the letters of license are rearranged

explanation.surface: A theatre needs a licence to stage the remainder of Hamlet.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's dying words are 'The rest is silence', so the definition borrows them.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's last line equates the rest with quiet, an absence of sound.

clue.text: What is uncommonly ousting peach?

indicators.note: uncommonly means in an unusual way, so the letters of ousting are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fruit is being pushed out in a strange way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peach' looks like the fruit; it is the verb meaning to inform on someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To peach is old slang for informing, and to sing is to confess to the police.

clue.text: Capital area for first couples in solar houses

indicators.note: the first pair of letters is taken from each of the following words

explanation.surface: An area of the capital has the first houses with solar panels.
explanation.walkthrough: Soho is a district of London's West End.
explanation.definitionFit: The London district is an area of the capital city.

clue.text: Supplier of some hard pieces for xylophone?

definitions.text: Supplier of some hard pieces for xylophone?

parts.words: Supplier of some hard pieces for xylophone?
parts.note: a very hard dark timber that could provide wooden bars for a percussion instrument

explanation.surface: A firm supplies difficult music for the xylophone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard pieces' looks like tricky music, but it means bits of hard wood; the dark tropical timber is also used for black piano keys.
explanation.definitionFit: A dense black tropical hardwood is suitable for instrument bars.

clue.text: Shut out in this manner

indicators.note: out means out of place, so the letters of shut are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is locked out like this.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb meaning so or like this.

clue.text: Cheerleader on strike is a very reticent sort

parts.note: the leader of the word cheer is its first letter
to lam is to hit hard

explanation.surface: A cheerleader joins a walkout but keeps very quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheerleader' is read as 'leader of cheer'. A shut-up shellfish gives 'to clam up', so a silent person is one.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight-lipped person is likened to a shellfish shut firmly.

clue.text: Despot and star turn

indicators.note: a turn moves the letters of star into a new order

explanation.surface: A tyrant and a celebrity perform an act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'star turn' looks like a headline act, but 'turn' rearranges STAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A Russian emperor was an absolute ruler.

clue.text: Great wave hitting Masefield's vessel gives a fair thrill

indicators.note: the wave hits the boat, the two words placed side by side

parts.note: a roller is a long heavy ocean wave
John Masefield's poem Cargoes has a 'dirty British coaster', a small coastal ship

explanation.surface: A big wave strikes a ship in a poem, giving a thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fair' is a funfair, not 'just'. John Masefield was a British Poet Laureate; his poem Cargoes features a coaster.
explanation.definitionFit: A switchback ride at a funfair is a source of thrills.

clue.text: Order to impress these frauds

indicators.note: order means arrange, so the letters of to impress are rearranged

explanation.surface: Frauds are ordered to impress.
explanation.walkthrough: The usual spelling ends -OR; this variant ends -ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Frauds who pretend to be others are impersonators.
